extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of early-18th-century periodical essays (coffee-house literate public); literary critics and playwright spectators
extracted.subtask_description: Short, satirical/observational periodical essays (The Tatler) offering commentary on manners, theatre, justice, and social types for the early-18th-century coffee-house readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pointing at particular persons when criticizing
rubrics_metrics.description: “the age you live in is such, that a good picture of any vice or virtue will infallibly be misrepresented; and though none will take the kind descriptions you make so much to themselves, as to wish well to the author, yet all will resent the ill characters you produce, out of fear of their own turn in the licence you must be obliged to take, if you point at particular persons.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admonition to writers: present vices/virtues in general or by character, not by naming or directly indicting real people, because readers will resent being implicated; restraint reduces personal offence and backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: If nothing commendable, forbear (do not be an inquisitor)
rubrics_metrics.description: “if I can find nothing to commend, I am silent, and will forbear the subject: for, though I am a reformer, I scorn to be an inquisitor.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical stance guidance: prefer silence over vicious or excessive condemnation; reform by example rather than by relentless personal prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic effectiveness: incidents (things) move the soul more than words
rubrics_metrics.description: “the soul is not to be moved by words, but things;” (example: 'The Earl of Essex' has 'not one good line, and yet a play which was never seen without drawing tears... the incidents in this drama are laid together so happily, that the spectator makes the play for himself').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating drama, prioritize plot incidents, circumstances, and situation-building over polished lines; powerful incidents can overcome poor diction or rhetorical weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor's physical presence and behaviour greatly affect a play's impact
rubrics_metrics.description: “the person and behaviour of Mr. Wilks has no small share in conducing to the popularity of the play; and when a handsome fellow is going to a more coarse exit than beheading, his shape and countenance make every tender one reprieve him...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of theatrical performance should account for the actor's embodiment (appearance, manner) as these can elicit audience sympathy beyond the text itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy genius: show a unifying motive (discernment of spirit)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The author's great address in showing covetousness the motive of the actions of the Puritan, the epicure, the gamester, and the trader... shows he had to a great perfection, that discernment of spirit, which constitutes a genius for comedy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mark of comic genius is revealing a single underlying motive that unifies varied characters and actions; expositional economy and moral insight into human motives strengthen comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should select subjects fitting their character and stature
rubrics_metrics.description: “to convince him, and all men of genius, of the folly of laying themselves out on such plans as are below their characters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to poets/writers: avoid pursuing trivial or undignified projects that are beneath one's established capacities or reputation; choose subjects appropriate to one's talents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal judge/judicial conduct: impartiality, legal knowledge, mercy where lawful
rubrics_metrics.description: “He considered justice as a cardinal virtue, not as a trade for maintenance... The criminal before him was always sure he stood before his country... his judge would wrest no law to destroy him, nor conceal any that could save him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard for judging (moral/legal): the judge should be learned, impartial, see through hypocrisy, apply laws to save when possible, and not treat justice as a means of personal maintenance or favour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antipatterns in magistrates: hypocrisy and selective enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of Trick-Track and Tearshift: one 'never spared a pickpocket, but was a companion to cheats'; the other 'would make compliments to wenches of quality, but certainly commit poor ones... sent [poor rogues] to gaol' for trivial matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of corrupt/partial magistrates: do not apply justice uniformly; they punish the poor while protecting or colluding with the well-connected—used as warnings of improper judicial behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical 'bite' technique (how to 'bite')
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnote definition: “A Biter is one who tells you a thing you have no reason to disbelieve in itself; and perhaps has given you, before he bit you, no reason to disbelieve it for his saying it; and if you give him credit, laughs in your face, and triumphs that he has deceived you.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method for satirical wit: present a plausible statement or bantering question (or a serious falsehood), gain the audience's credence, then reveal the deception—this 'bite' depends on initial plausibility and the element of surprise.
